    Your recordings

    Send recordings here from WhatsApp or Voice Memos

    On an iPhone or iPad, a Shortcut puts anything you share into an Inbox folder in iCloud Drive, named with who's singing and the day. Then + Add recordings and pick it from the folder; the name fills in the details. Set it up once:

    1. In iCloud Drive › Sangeet Diary, make a folder called Inbox.
    2. In the Shortcuts app, tap + and name it Send to Sangeet Diary. Tap ⓘ and turn on Show in Share Sheet.
    3. Add Ask for Input (Text), prompt Who's singing?, default answer Teacher.
    4. Add another Ask for Input (Text), prompt What is it?, e.g. Bhairav class.
    5. Add Format Date: Current Date, Custom format yyyy-MM-dd, no time.
    6. Add Set Name on the Shortcut Input, to: the first answer, space, dash, space, the date, space, dash, space, the second answer. It reads like Teacher - 2026-11-07 - Bhairav class.
    7. Add Save File to iCloud Drive › Sangeet Diary › Inbox, with Ask Where to Save off.
    8. Add Show Notification: In your inbox. In Sangeet Diary, + Add recordings.

    Now in WhatsApp (a voice note or audio: Forward, then the share icon), Voice Memos or Files, share it to Send to Sangeet Diary. If a WhatsApp voice note won't open here, add Encode Media (Audio Only) before Set Name. Picking the same file again won't add it twice.

    Sing freely

    Your line is rose, and takes the svara’s colour where you hold one. Held notes are named with how far off they are (within 10¢ is in tune) and how steady. Solid lines are the rāg’s svaras, dashed ones the rest. Use headphones, so the mic hears you and not the tanpura.

    Phrase by phrase

    Find them places each written line where it’s first sung (? where it’s a guess: loop it to check); or mark one by hand. Each then sits along the top of the graph with its svaras where they’re sung, and a tap there loops it (the strip shows once there’s a line in it). Faint svaras weren’t clearly heard, so their place is a guess.

    Tap to jump there · drag to move along · pinch or ⌘/Ctrl + scroll to zoom · Space plays · L loops the phrase · double tap the svara names to see the whole range. The strip underneath is the whole recording.

    the voice: ink as it moves, the svara's colour where it holds oneheld svara: fainter when less sure, ? when unsureandolan / gamakkaṇ: the svara touchedunclear movement

    How this is worked out

    Pitch. The voice's pitch is measured every 10 ms (the YIN method). Svaras sit where they're sung in practice (Ga and Dha a touch lower than on a piano), and a held note is called in tune within about a sixth of a semitone of there, a little high or low within a third, and high or low beyond that. Turn on Details for the exact numbers: Hz, the Western note, and cents (100 cents make a semitone).

    Notes and ornaments. A svara is named only where the voice settles (steady within half a semitone for 0.1 s or more, and level, not gliding). Everything else is shown as movement: a meend glides 1.5 semitones or more one way; a kaṇ touches beyond both neighbouring notes for under 0.25 s; an andolan swings slowly (0.2–0.8 s each way) between the same top and bottom; a gamak swings faster and wider. Smaller shakes are the voice's vibrato and stay part of the note. Anything else is hatched and marked “?”.

    Confidence. Sure: held 0.2 s or more, within a third of a semitone, clearly sung. Fairly sure: shorter or a little off. Unsure: very short, far off-centre, quiet (between phrases an instrument may be what's heard), outside the rāg's scale, or a likely octave slip.

    Limits. It measures; it doesn't listen the way you do. A drone or harmonium under the voice can pull the reading for a moment, and very fast tāns are traced only roughly. Your ear and your teacher have the last word.
